html:
The Songhai are a people of the middle Niger River, around Gao and the Niger bend, in what are now Mali and Niger. The map shows their lands from 1492 to 1800: first the Songhai Empire at its height, then the smaller states that followed it.

A Songhai kingdom existed around Gao from the 800s or earlier, trading across the Sahara, and was for a time subject to the Mali Empire. In the later 1400s it became the largest empire West Africa had seen:

  • Sonni Ali took Timbuktu and Djenné by war;
  • Askia Muhammad I organised it into provinces and made Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.

In 1591 an army sent by the Saadi sultan of Morocco crossed the Sahara with firearms and won the Battle of Tondibi. The empire broke apart. The Moroccans and their descendants, the Arma, ruled Timbuktu and Gao as pashas, while scholars such as Ahmad Baba were carried off to Marrakesh. Songhai princes held out downstream in the Dendi Kingdom in what is now Niger, which lasted into the 1800s.

Without a strong state the Niger bend was raided by Tuareg and Bambara, and trade shifted toward the Atlantic coast. The Songhai still live along the river, many as farmers and fishers.
